[ASSISTANT_SAID] The memory and legacy of the atomic bombing of Hiroshima have been passed down through generations by various means, including:  
[ASSISTANT_SAID] 1. Oral history: Survivors of the bombing, also called hibakusha, have shared their stories and experiences of the event with their children and grandchildren.  
[ASSISTANT_SAID] 2. Literature: Several works of Japanese literature have been dedicated to the atomic bombings of Hiroshima and Nagasaki, such as "Black Rain" by Masuji Ibuse, "Barefoot Gen" by Keiji Nakazawa, and "Hiroshima" by John Hersey.  
[ASSISTANT_SAID] 3. Memorials and museums: The Hiroshima Peace Memorial Museum and the Peace Memorial Park are two main sites that commemorate the bombing and educate visitors on its horrific effects.  
[ASSISTANT_SAID] 4. Film and media: Several films and documentaries, such as "White Light/Black Rain: The Destruction of Hiroshima and Nagasaki" and "Hiroshima Mon Amour," have been made about the bombings.  
[ASSISTANT_SAID] 5. Education: The atomic bombing of Hiroshima is taught to Japanese school children as part of their history curriculum.  
[ASSISTANT_SAID] Overall, the memory and legacy of the atomic bombing of Hiroshima have been kept alive by the collective efforts of survivors, academics, writers, and artists.
